Both contain $p$, so they lie in the same set, say $U$. Then $V \cap (A \cup B) = \varnothing$, a contradiction. $\blacksquare$
$A$ and $B$ are connected, so their union is: connectedness adds up.
lines.why: It does not in general: $[0, 1]$ and $[2, 3]$ are connected but their union is not. The common point is needed.

items.prose: On $X = \{a, b, c\}$ take the chains $\tau = \{\varnothing, \{a\}, \{a, b\}, X\}$ and $\tau' = \{\varnothing, \{b\}, \{b, c\}, X\}$.
items.question: How many bijections $X \to X$ carry $\tau$ onto $\tau'$?

feedback.generic: Not quite. The open singleton must go to the open singleton.

byKey.all: 6 counts every bijection. Most do not carry $\{a\}$ to $\{b\}$.
byKey.none: The two chains have the same shape, so a relabelling exists.

explain.text: $\{a\}$ must go to $\{b\}$, then $\{a, b\}$ to $\{b, c\}$, which forces $b \mapsto c$ and $c \mapsto a$. So exactly 1 bijection works, and $\tau \cong \tau'$.

items.prose: The homeomorphism of l7 sends the square to the disc by $P \mapsto P \cdot \tfrac{d_\infty(0, P)}{d_2(0, P)}$. Its inverse multiplies by $\tfrac{d_2}{d_\infty}$.
items.question: Which point of the square maps to $P' = (0.6, 0.8)$? Give its first coordinate.

feedback.correct: Right. $(0.75, 1)$, on the square's top edge.

byKey.same: You left $P'$ unchanged. It lies on the circle; its preimage lies on the square.
byKey.forward: You applied the forward map again: $0.6 \times 0.8$.

explain.text: $d_2(0, P') = 1$ and $d_\infty(0, P') = 0.8$, so the preimage is $(0.6, 0.8) / 0.8 = (0.75, 1)$. It lies on the top edge, as a rim point must.

items.prose: (After Sutherland, chapters 9 and 12.) Let $X$ be an infinite set with the cofinite topology. Its open sets are $\varnothing$ and the sets with finite complement.
items.question: Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.why: Two non-empty open sets each miss finitely many points, so they meet.

options.text: Some metric on $X$ gives these open sets
options.why: Every metric space is Hausdorff, and this space is not.
A singleton has infinite complement, so it is not open.

feedback.correct: Right. Connected, singletons closed, not Hausdorff.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Use that non-empty open sets have finite complements.

explain.text: Two disjoint non-empty open sets cannot exist, so $X$ is connected and not Hausdorff, hence not metric. Each $X \setminus \{x\}$ has finite complement, so it is open and $\{x\}$ is closed.

items.title: The intermediate value theorem from connectedness
items.prompt: Prove three things. (1) If $f : X \to Y$ is continuous and $X$ is connected, then $f(X)$ is connected. (2) A connected subset $C$ of $\mathbb{R}$ is an interval: if $x < y < z$ with $x, z \in C$, then $y \in C$. (3) Optional, one more point: deduce the intermediate value theorem: a continuous $f : [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}$ takes every value between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$. You may use that $[a, b]$ is connected.
items.model:
**(1) Images.** Suppose $U, V$ are open in $f(X)$, disjoint, non-empty, with $U \cup V = f(X)$. Write $U = U' \cap f(X)$ and $V = V' \cap f(X)$ with $U', V'$ open in $Y$. Then $f^{-1}(U) = f^{-1}(U')$ and $f^{-1}(V) = f^{-1}(V')$ are open in $X$ by continuity. They are disjoint because $U$ and $V$ are; non-empty because $U, V \subseteq f(X)$ are non-empty; and they cover $X$ because $U \cup V = f(X)$. That separates $X$, a contradiction. So $f(X)$ is connected.

**(2) Intervals.** Let $C \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be connected, $x < y < z$ with $x, z \in C$, and suppose $y \notin C$. Put $U = (-\infty, y) \cap C$ and $V = (y, \infty) \cap C$. Both are open in $C$, disjoint, and cover $C$ since $y \notin C$. $x \in U$ and $z \in V$, so both are non-empty. That separates $C$, a contradiction. So $y \in C$, and $C$ is an interval.

**(3) The theorem.** $[a, b]$ is connected, so by (1) $f([a, b])$ is connected, and by (2) it is an interval. It contains $f(a)$ and $f(b)$, so it contains every $y$ between them: $y = f(c)$ for some $c \in [a, b]$. $\blacksquare$

The connected domain is needed. On $[0, 1] \cup [2, 3]$, the map equal to 0 then 1 is continuous and misses $\tfrac12$.

rubric.text: (1) Pulls a separation of $f(X)$ back to open sets of $X$ by continuity.
(1) Checks the preimages are disjoint, non-empty and cover $X$, and concludes.
(2) Separates $C$ by the rays on either side of a missing $y$, with both pieces non-empty.
(3) Combines (1) and (2) with the connectedness of $[a, b]$ to get $f(c) = y$.
